passages.title: Birds That Chose the Sea
passages.passage:
Ask a child to draw a penguin and you will probably get a black-and-white bird standing on ice. The picture is not wrong, but it is only part of the story. Of the eighteen kinds of penguin alive today, just a few spend their lives in Antarctica. Others live on the beaches of South Africa, the rocky islands of New Zealand, and even the Galápagos Islands, which sit right on the equator. What every penguin shares is not the cold, but the sea.

Penguins are birds, yet they cannot fly. Over millions of years, their wings became short and stiff, more like paddles than wings. On land this makes them slow and rather clumsy, which is why they seem so funny to us. Under water, however, they are as fast and graceful as any fish. A penguin's body is shaped like a torpedo, and it steers with its feet and tail. Some species can dive deeper than a hundred metres and hold their breath for many minutes.

Staying warm in cold water is a serious problem, and penguins solve it in several ways. Their feathers are small and packed tightly together, so that water cannot reach the skin. Under the feathers is a thick layer of fat. Emperor penguins, which live through the Antarctic winter, go one step further: thousands of birds stand pressed against one another in a huge group, and they take turns moving from the cold outside to the warm centre.

Sadly, many penguin populations are shrinking. Fishing boats take the small fish that penguins depend on, oil spills damage their feathers, and warmer seas push their food further away. Scientists who count penguins each year say that some colonies are half the size they were thirty years ago. The birds that once seemed so far from us are now telling us something about the health of the oceans we all share.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why penguins can only survive in Antarctica
How penguins are built for life in the sea, and the dangers they now face
The reason penguins lost the ability to fly
How scientists count penguin colonies every year
questions.explanation: Each paragraph is about penguins and the sea: where they live, how they swim, how they keep warm in the water and what is harming them. Antarctica, flying and counting are single details, and the first option contradicts paragraph 1.

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, what do all penguins have in common?
options: They are found on the equator.
They live in very cold places.
questions.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph 1 says directly: 'What every penguin shares is not the cold, but the sea.' The islands and the equator apply only to some species.

questions.q: The word 'clumsy' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts penguins on land ('slow and rather clumsy', 'funny') with penguins in the water ('fast and graceful'). The opposite of graceful is awkward.

questions.q: What can be inferred about emperor penguins?
options: They cannot dive as deep as other species.
They are the only penguins with a layer of fat.
They face colder conditions than most other penguins.
They never leave the centre of the group.
questions.explanation: Emperor penguins 'live through the Antarctic winter' and 'go one step further' than the fat and feathers all penguins have, which suggests their cold is more extreme. The passage says the birds take turns in the centre, so they do leave it.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, 'penguins solve it in several ways' — what does 'it' refer to?
questions.explanation: The sentence begins 'Staying warm in cold water is a serious problem', and 'it' is that problem. The feathers and fat are the ways it is solved, not the thing being solved.

questions.q: Some penguin colonies are now half the size they were three decades ago.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says scientists report that 'some colonies are half the size they were thirty years ago'. Thirty years is three decades.

questions.q: Oil spills are the greatest danger that penguins face.
questions.explanation: Oil spills are listed as one of three dangers, alongside fishing and warmer seas, but the passage never ranks them. There is no information about which is the greatest.

passages.title: Thirty Minutes with a Broken Chain
passages.passage:
The chain came off halfway up the hill on Tran Phu Street, and then, with a sound like a dropped spoon, it snapped in two. I was already late for school. For a moment I stood there in the heat, holding a bicycle that had suddenly become nothing more than a heavy piece of metal.

The bike was not new. It had belonged to my older cousin, and before that to someone in his neighbourhood. The paint was scratched, the bell did not ring, and the back brake only worked if you pulled it with both hands. My mother had promised that I could have a new one when I started grade 10, so my first thought that morning was simple: leave it, walk to school, and wait for September.

Instead, I pushed it to the repair stand at the corner. The old man who ran it, Mr Bay, looked at the chain and then looked at me. 'I can fix this in ten minutes,' he said, 'or you can fix it in thirty, and then you'll never need me again.' I wanted to say that I was late, but something in the way he said it made me put my bag down.

He did not do the work for me. He showed me how to find the broken link, how to push the pin out with a small tool, and how to join the two ends again. My fingers were black with oil, and I got to school in the middle of second period with a note from nobody. But the chain held.

That was two years ago. I did get the new bicycle, and it is lighter and faster and the bell works. Yet on Sundays I still ride the old one to the market. When it breaks, and it does, I take out the tools that Mr Bay sold me for the price of a bowl of noodles. I have learned that a thing is only broken until somebody decides to understand it.

questions.q: What is the story mainly about?
options: A morning that taught the narrator the value of repairing things
The daily work of an old repairman named Mr Bay
Why the narrator was late for school one day
How the narrator finally received a new bicycle for grade 10
questions.explanation: The broken chain, Mr Bay's lesson and the final sentence about understanding broken things all point to one idea: learning to repair rather than replace. The new bicycle and the lateness are details.

questions.q: What was wrong with the bicycle before the chain broke?
options: The front brake did not work at all.
The chain had already been repaired once.
The paint was new but the tyres were old.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists scratched paint, a bell that did not ring and a weak back brake. It is the back brake, not the front, and nothing is said about the chain or the tyres.

questions.q: Why did Mr Bay offer the narrator a choice?
options: He did not have the tool needed for the job.
He was too busy to repair the chain himself.
He wanted the narrator to be able to repair the bike alone in future.
He was not sure the narrator could pay him.
questions.explanation: His words 'then you'll never need me again' show his aim was to make the narrator independent. He clearly had the tool, since he later sold the narrator a set.

questions.q: The phrase 'the chain held' in paragraph 4 means that the chain
questions.explanation: 'Held' here means it did not break again. The word 'But' contrasts the messy, late arrival with the one thing that went right: the repair worked.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention 'a note from nobody'?
options: to show that the narrator had no written excuse for being late
to show that Mr Bay refused to write a note
to show that the teacher did not mind lateness
to show that the narrator forgot to bring the note
questions.explanation: A student who arrives late normally brings a note from a parent or doctor. 'A note from nobody' is a humorous way of saying the narrator arrived with no excuse at all.

questions.q: The narrator still uses the old bicycle.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 says 'on Sundays I still ride the old one to the market', even though the narrator now owns a new bicycle.

questions.q: Mr Bay gave the narrator a set of tools for free.
questions.explanation: The tools were 'sold' to the narrator 'for the price of a bowl of noodles'. That is cheap, but it is not free.

passages.title: The Library in My Grandmother's Head
passages.passage:
My grandmother has never written anything longer than a shopping list, but she carries a whole library in her head. Every evening after dinner, when the dishes are done and the television has been switched off, she settles into the wooden chair by the window and begins. 'Did I ever tell you about the year the river came into the kitchen?' She has, many times. We listen anyway.

When I was small, I thought her stories were simply entertainment, like cartoons. There was the one about the buffalo that walked into the classroom, the one about my grandfather arriving for their first meeting on a borrowed bicycle with one pedal missing, and the one about the flood, which is the longest and the saddest. I knew them so well that I could correct her if she changed a detail.

It was a history project in grade 8 that made me see them differently. Our teacher asked us to interview an older relative about life in the past. I recorded my grandmother for an hour on my phone, expecting to hear the same tales. But this time I was listening for facts. How much did rice cost? How far away was the nearest doctor? How did people know the flood was coming? Her stories, it turned out, were full of answers. The buffalo story was really about a school with no walls. The bicycle story was about a time when a bicycle was the most valuable thing a family owned.

My grandmother is eighty-three now, and some days she asks me the same question twice. The doctor says this is normal at her age, but it frightens me a little. So I keep recording. I have more than twenty hours saved, and I have started writing them down, exactly as she tells them, with the pauses and the jokes.

She laughed when I told her what I was doing. 'Nobody wants old stories,' she said. I think she is wrong. A story is one of the few things that becomes more valuable the more it is given away.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: A flood that once reached the family's kitchen
Why elderly people often repeat themselves
How the narrator completed a grade 8 history project
How the narrator came to see a grandmother's stories as valuable family history
questions.explanation: The passage moves from seeing the stories as 'entertainment' to discovering they were 'full of answers' about the past, and ends with the narrator saving them. The project, the flood and the repeated questions are details.

questions.q: What did the teacher ask the students to do for the history project?
options: Find out how much rice used to cost
Write down every story their grandparents told
Interview an older family member about life in the past
Record a relative for at least twenty hours
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states the task: 'interview an older relative about life in the past'. The twenty hours and the writing down came later, by the narrator's own choice, and the price of rice was just one question asked.

questions.q: What does the narrator suggest about the grandmother's memory?
options: It is as strong as it has always been.
It has already been completely lost.
The doctor believes it is unusual for her age.
questions.explanation: She 'asks me the same question twice' on some days, which 'frightens' the narrator, and this is why the narrator 'keeps recording'. The doctor calls it normal, and she can still tell her stories, so it is not lost.

questions.q: The word 'tales' in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: The narrator expected 'to hear the same tales', meaning the stories already described in paragraph 2. The contrast in the next sentence is with 'facts', so 'facts' cannot be the meaning.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, 'made me see them differently' — what does 'them' refer to?
questions.explanation: 'Them' points back to the stories described throughout paragraph 2. The rest of paragraph 3 explains how those same stories turned out to be full of facts.

questions.q: Why does the writer end with the sentence 'A story is one of the few things that becomes more valuable the more it is given away'?
options: to suggest that the recordings should be sold
to warn that the stories will soon be forgotten
to disagree with the grandmother's view that nobody wants old stories
to explain why the grandmother laughed
questions.explanation: The sentence comes straight after 'I think she is wrong', so it gives the reason the narrator disagrees with 'Nobody wants old stories'. Nothing is said about selling the recordings.

questions.q: The grandmother has written some of her stories down herself.
questions.explanation: The first sentence says she 'has never written anything longer than a shopping list'. It is the narrator, not the grandmother, who has started writing the stories down.

passages.title: Ninety Minutes in the Rain
passages.passage:
The rain started during the warm-up and did not stop for the whole afternoon. By the time the referee blew his whistle for the final of the district schools' cup, the pitch behind Nguyen Du Secondary was less a football field than a shallow brown lake with white lines painted on it.

I was the goalkeeper, which on a dry day is the loneliest position on the pitch. In the rain it is the busiest. The ball would not roll; it stopped dead in the puddles or skidded off at strange angles. Twice in the first half, a shot that should have been easy to catch slipped through my gloves like a bar of soap. We were two goals down at half-time, and I could not look at my teammates.

Our coach, Mr Hung, did not shout. He handed out dry towels, which were wet within a minute, and said only one thing: 'Stop trying to play the game you practised. Play the game that is in front of you.' It sounded like a line from a film, but it turned out to be practical advice. In the second half we stopped passing along the ground, where the ball died, and started lifting it over the puddles. Our tallest defender was moved up front, because in that mud nobody could turn quickly and height mattered more than speed.

We scored in the sixtieth minute and again in the eighty-fifth. The second goal came from a corner that the wind carried straight into the net, and for a moment nobody was sure whether it counted. It did. The match ended two–two, and the cup was shared, because the organisers decided that nobody could take a penalty shoot-out seriously in that weather.

I have played in better matches since, and won some of them properly. But when people ask me about football, that is the afternoon I describe: the cold, the mud, the towels that were no use, and the strange discovery that a plan is only good until the weather changes.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: A coach's half-time speech that came from a film
How a school team won the district cup in a penalty shoot-out
A rainy final in which a team learned to change its plan
Why goalkeepers dislike playing in wet weather
questions.explanation: The story builds to the coach's advice, the change of tactics in the second half and the final lesson that 'a plan is only good until the weather changes'. There was no shoot-out, and the speech and the goalkeeper's problems are details.

questions.q: Why was the tallest defender moved forward?
options: Because he had already scored in the first half
Because the wind was blowing towards the goal
Because he was the fastest player on the team
Because players could not turn quickly in the mud
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains: 'in that mud nobody could turn quickly and height mattered more than speed'. The wind is mentioned only for the second goal, and the team did not score in the first half.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the two first-half goals?
options: The narrator feels partly responsible for them.
The referee should not have allowed them.
They were the result of the wet towels.
questions.explanation: The narrator says shots that 'should have been easy to catch' slipped through and 'I could not look at my teammates', which shows a feeling of guilt. Nothing suggests the referee was wrong or that corners were involved.

questions.q: The word 'skidded' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: The ball either 'stopped dead' or 'skidded off at strange angles', so skidding is the opposite of stopping: sliding quickly and uncontrollably across the wet surface.

questions.q: In paragraph 4, the short sentence 'It did.' means that
questions.explanation: The sentence before says 'nobody was sure whether it counted'. 'It did' answers that doubt: the goal was allowed, which is why the score became two–two.

questions.q: The final was played on the narrator's own school pitch.
questions.explanation: The pitch was 'behind Nguyen Du Secondary', but the passage never says which school the narrator attends. We cannot tell whether it was a home pitch.

questions.q: The narrator's team lost the final.
questions.explanation: The match 'ended two–two, and the cup was shared'. The team did not win outright, but it certainly did not lose.
